concept.name: LiteLLM
concept.title: LiteLLM: one interface for many language models
concept.definition: LiteLLM is an open-source toolkit that lets you call 100+ language-model providers through one OpenAI-compatible interface. Use it as a Python library in your app, or as a proxy so any OpenAI client can reach many backends.
concept.problem: Each model vendor has its own API, keys, errors, and request shape. Using several providers, or switching later, means rewriting application code and juggling separate integrations.

nodes.label: Your App
nodes.caption: chatbot, agent, or script
nodes.description: The code that needs a language model. It should speak one request shape, not a different SDK for every vendor.

nodes.label: Python SDK
nodes.caption: library in your process
nodes.description: A Python library you import. Your app calls one completion-style function; LiteLLM talks to the chosen provider from inside the same process.

nodes.label: Proxy Server
nodes.caption: shared AI gateway
nodes.description: A self-hosted HTTP service. Any OpenAI-compatible client points at the proxy URL. Teams use this when many apps should share routing, keys, and spend tracking.

nodes.label: Unified API
nodes.caption: OpenAI format in and out
nodes.description: LiteLLM accepts the OpenAI request shape, translates it to the target provider, and returns a consistent OpenAI-shaped response. Switching models is a config or model-name change, not a rewrite of your client.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.caption: retry, fallback, balance
nodes.description: The Router can send traffic across deployments, retry failures, and fall back to another model if a provider is down or rate-limited.

nodes.label: Spend and Logs
nodes.caption: cost and traces
nodes.description: LiteLLM can record usage and estimated cost per call, and emit logs or traces to observability tools. The proxy also attributes spend to teams and virtual keys.

nodes.label: Model Providers
nodes.caption: OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and more
nodes.description: The actual model vendors and hosted endpoints. LiteLLM keeps their different APIs behind one interface so your app does not integrate each one separately.

groups.label: LiteLLM — one interface for many models
groups.description: The SDK and the proxy both expose the same unified API. The Router and spend tracking sit behind that API.

chapters.title: Many models, many APIs
chapters.explanation: Your app needs language models from several vendors. Each vendor has its own request shape, authentication, and errors. Without a translator, every new provider is a new integration.
takeaways: Their APIs are not the same
Your app should not speak all of them

chapters.title: One OpenAI-compatible interface
chapters.explanation: LiteLLM sits in the middle. Your app sends an OpenAI-style request. LiteLLM translates it to the chosen provider and returns a consistent OpenAI-shaped response, so switching models does not mean rewriting the client.
takeaways: OpenAI-compatible means one request and response shape

chapters.title: Library or proxy
chapters.explanation: There are two ways to use that interface. Import the Python SDK when one app wants a library. Run the Proxy Server when many apps, languages, or teams should share one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
takeaways: The SDK lives inside one Python process
The proxy is a shared HTTP gateway
Both present the same OpenAI-style API

chapters.title: Route, recover, and see spend
chapters.explanation: The Router can retry a failed call and fall back to another model if a provider is down or rate-limited. LiteLLM can also record usage and cost. On the proxy, that spend can be attributed across apps and teams.
takeaways: Spend logs answer what a call cost
The proxy can share that visibility across teams

contextCards.title: How the pieces fit
points: Your app sends one OpenAI-style request.
The SDK or the proxy hands that request to LiteLLM's unified API.
The Router forwards the call to a model provider and LiteLLM can record the spend.

contextCards.title: What the neighbors do
points: The Python SDK is a library one app imports. The Proxy Server is a gateway many clients call.
The Router chooses among deployments and can retry or fall back.
Model providers are the vendors that actually run the models.

contextCards.title: Why this exists
points: Stop writing a new client for every vendor API.
Change models without starting a new application project.
Keep working if one provider fails, and see what each call cost.
